results.title: Mixed differential along the empty list
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $\sigma$ be an index type, and let $p \in R[x_s : s \in \sigma]$. The mixed differential of $p$ along the empty list of indices is $p$ itself.

results.title: Mixed differential along a list with a given first index
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $\sigma$ be an index type, let $i \in \sigma$, let $L$ be a finite list of indices in $\sigma$, and let $p \in R[x_s : s \in \sigma]$. The mixed differential of $p$ along the list that starts with $i$ and continues with $L$ equals the mixed differential along $L$ of $p - \partial_i p$, where $\partial_i$ is the partial derivative with respect to $x_i$.

results.title: The mixed differential ignores the order of the indices
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $\sigma$ be an index type, and let $p \in R[x_s : s \in \sigma]$. If two finite lists $L$ and $L'$ of indices in $\sigma$ are permutations of each other, then the mixed differentials of $p$ along $L$ and along $L'$ are equal.

results.title: Mixed differential along a concatenated list
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $\sigma$ be an index type, let $p \in R[x_s : s \in \sigma]$, and let $L$ and $L'$ be finite lists of indices in $\sigma$. The mixed differential of $p$ along the concatenation of $L$ followed by $L'$ equals the mixed differential along $L'$ of the mixed differential of $p$ along $L$.

results.title: Partial derivatives commute with the mixed differential
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $i \in \sigma$, let $L$ be a finite list of indices in $\sigma$, and let $p \in R[x_s : s \in \sigma]$. Writing $\partial_i$ for the partial derivative with respect to $x_i$, the partial derivative $\partial_i$ of the mixed differential of $p$ along $L$ equals the mixed differential along $L$ of $\partial_i p$.

results.title: Boolean encoding of sign matrices
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: For a natural number $n$, a sign matrix of order $n$ is encoded as an $n \times n$ matrix with entries in the Booleans $\{\mathrm{true}, \mathrm{false}\}$, whose rows and columns are indexed by $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$.

results.title: Real sign matrix of a Boolean matrix
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The realization of a Boolean $n \times n$ matrix $A$ is the real $n \times n$ matrix whose $(i, j)$ entry is $-1$ if $A_{ij}$ is true and $1$ if $A_{ij}$ is false.

results.title: Realized sign matrices have entries $\pm 1$
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every Boolean $n \times n$ matrix $A$ and all indices $i, j$, the $(i, j)$ entry of the real realization of $A$ is $1$ or $-1$.

results.title: Boolean matrices realize exactly the sign matrices
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Send each $n \times n$ Boolean matrix to the real matrix whose entry is $-1$ where the Boolean entry is true and $1$ where it is false. A real $n \times n$ matrix $M$ arises in this way if and only if every entry of $M$ is $1$ or $-1$.

results.title: Condition number of a square real matrix
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a real $n \times n$ matrix $A$, let $\sigma_0 \ge \sigma_1 \ge \dots$ be the singular values of $A$ acting on Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^n$, indexed from $0$ and extended by $\sigma_i = 0$ for $i \ge n$. The condition number of $A$, an element of $[0, \infty]$, is $\infty$ if $\sigma_{n-1} = 0$ and $\sigma_0 / \sigma_{n-1}$ otherwise, where $n - 1$ is read as $0$ when $n = 0$.

results.title: Minimum condition number of sign matrices
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a positive integer $n$, the minimum condition number of order $n$ is the least condition number of a real $n \times n$ sign matrix, that is, a matrix all of whose entries are $1$ or $-1$; the minimum is taken over the finitely many such matrices.

results.title: Infinite condition number from a vanishing singular value
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $A$ be a real $n \times n$ matrix with singular values $\sigma_0 \ge \sigma_1 \ge \dots$ on Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^n$, indexed from $0$ and extended by zeros, where $n - 1$ is read as $0$ when $n = 0$. If $\sigma_{n-1} = 0$, then the condition number of $A$ is $\infty$.

results.title: Condition number as a singular-value ratio
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $A$ be a real $n \times n$ matrix with singular values $\sigma_0 \ge \sigma_1 \ge \dots$ on Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^n$, indexed from $0$ and extended by zeros, where $n - 1$ is read as $0$ when $n = 0$. If $\sigma_{n-1} \ne 0$, then the condition number of $A$ equals $\sigma_0 / \sigma_{n-1}$.

results.title: The zero matrix has infinite condition number
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every natural number $n$, the condition number of the real $n \times n$ zero matrix is $\infty$; this includes the $0 \times 0$ matrix.

results.title: The minimum condition number is attained
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every positive integer $n$, there is an $n \times n$ Boolean matrix whose realization as a real sign matrix ($-1$ for true, $1$ for false) has condition number equal to the minimum condition number of order $n$.

results.title: Condition numbers are at least one
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every natural number $n$ and every real $n \times n$ matrix $A$, the condition number of $A$ is at least $1$.

results.title: The minimum condition number is at least one
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every positive integer $n$, the minimum condition number of the real $n \times n$ sign matrices is at least $1$.

results.title: Condition number of the order-one identity
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The condition number of the $1 \times 1$ real identity matrix is $1$.

results.title: Minimum condition number of order one
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The minimum condition number of order $1$ is $1$: the least condition number of a $1 \times 1$ real sign matrix is $1$.

results.title: Subpolynomial sequences
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A sequence $f \colon \mathbb{N} \to [0, \infty)$ is subpolynomial when for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ we have $f(n) = o(n^{\varepsilon})$ as $n \to \infty$.

results.title: Admissible decay exponents
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A real number $\alpha$ is an admissible exponent when there is a subpolynomial sequence $f \colon \mathbb{N} \to [0, \infty)$ such that for every positive integer $n$ the minimum condition number $\kappa_n$ of the real $n \times n$ sign matrices satisfies $\kappa_n = 1 + f(n) / n^{\alpha}$, as an equality in $[0, \infty]$.

results.title: Decay exponent of minimum sign-matrix condition numbers
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The decay exponent is the supremum, taken in the extended reals $[-\infty, \infty]$, of the set of admissible exponents $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$.

results.title: Hadamard hypothesis
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The Hadamard hypothesis is the proposition that for every natural number $n$ divisible by $4$ there is an $n \times n$ Hadamard matrix with integer entries, that is, an integer matrix $H$ with all entries $\pm 1$ such that $H H^{\mathsf{T}} = H^{\mathsf{T}} H = n I$.

results.title: Symmetric conference matrices
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A real $n \times n$ matrix $C$ is a symmetric conference matrix when $n \ge 2$, $C^{\mathsf{T}} = C$, every diagonal entry of $C$ is $0$, every off-diagonal entry of $C$ is $1$ or $-1$, and $C C^{\mathsf{T}} = (n - 1) I$, where $I$ is the identity matrix.

results.title: Adding the identity to a symmetric conference matrix gives a sign matrix
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If $C$ is a real $n \times n$ symmetric conference matrix and $I$ is the $n \times n$ identity matrix, then there is a Boolean $n \times n$ matrix whose realization as a real sign matrix equals $C + I$.

results.title: Divisor-gap sums (Erdős Problem 884)
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The statement that there is a real constant $C > 0$ such that for every positive integer $n$, if $d_1 < d_2 < \dots < d_t$ are all the divisors of $n$ in increasing order, then $\sum_{1 \le i < j \le t} \frac{1}{d_j - d_i} \le C \left(1 + \sum_{1 \le i < t} \frac{1}{d_{i+1} - d_i}\right)$.

results.title: Erdős Problem 884 is false (Larsen)
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every real constant $C > 0$ there is a positive integer $n$ whose divisors $d_1 < d_2 < \dots < d_t$, listed in increasing order, satisfy $\sum_{1 \le i < j \le t} \frac{1}{d_j - d_i} > C \left(1 + \sum_{1 \le i < t} \frac{1}{d_{i+1} - d_i}\right)$.

results.title: Kummer's theorem for regular primes
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $p$ be an odd prime and let $K$ be a $p$-th cyclotomic field over $\mathbb{Q}$ (a number field generated over $\mathbb{Q}$ by a primitive $p$-th root of unity). If $p$ does not divide the class number of $K$, then Fermat's Last Theorem holds for the exponent $p$: there are no positive integers $a, b, c$ with $a^p + b^p = c^p$.

results.title: Wieferich's criterion for the first case of Fermat's Last Theorem
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $p$ be a prime that is not a Wieferich prime, that is, $p^2 \nmid 2^{p-1} - 1$. Then there are no integers $x, y, z$ with $p \nmid xyz$ and $x^p + y^p = z^p$.

results.title: Skula–Dobson–Ichimura congruence for the Fermat quotient of $2$
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $p$ be an odd prime and $N$ a positive integer with $p \nmid N$. Write $q_p(2) = (2^{p-1} - 1)/p$ for the Fermat quotient of $2$, and for integers $i \ge 0$ and $M \ge 1$ let $s_p(i, M) \in \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$ be the sum of $m^{-1}$ over the integers $m$ with $0 < m < p$ and $ip/M < m < (i+1)p/M$. Then $(N + 1)\, q_p(2) \equiv -\sum_{0 \le j < N/2} s_p(2j, 2N) \pmod{p}$.

results.title: Hurwitz rounding to the nearest Gaussian integer
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a complex number $z$, let $[z] = m + n i$, where $m = \lfloor \operatorname{Re} z + 1/2 \rfloor$ and $n = \lfloor \operatorname{Im} z + 1/2 \rfloor$; that is, the real and imaginary parts of $z$ are rounded to the nearest integer, with halves rounded up. Then $[z]$ is a Gaussian integer nearest to $z$.

results.title: Iterates of the Hurwitz algorithm
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a complex number $z$, the Hurwitz iterates are $z_0 = z$ and $z_{n+1} = (z_n - [z_n])^{-1}$ for $n \ge 0$, where $[u]$ is the Gaussian integer nearest to $u$, obtained by rounding the real and imaginary parts of $u$ to the nearest integer with halves rounded up, and where the inverse of $0$ is taken to be $0$.

results.title: Partial quotients of the Hurwitz expansion
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $z$ be a complex number with Hurwitz iterates $z_0 = z, z_1, z_2, \dots$. For $n \ge 0$, the $n$-th partial quotient is $a_n = [z_n]$, the Gaussian integer nearest to $z_n$, obtained by rounding the real and imaginary parts of $z_n$ to the nearest integer with halves rounded up.

results.title: Consecutive pairs of Hurwitz convergents
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $z$ be a complex number with Hurwitz partial quotients $a_0, a_1, a_2, \dots$. This is the sequence whose term for $n \ge 0$ is the pair of pairs of complex numbers $((P_{n-1}, Q_{n-1}), (P_n, Q_n))$, where $P_{-1} = 1$, $Q_{-1} = 0$, $P_0 = a_0$, $Q_0 = 1$, and $P_{n+1} = a_{n+1} P_n + P_{n-1}$ and $Q_{n+1} = a_{n+1} Q_n + Q_{n-1}$ for $n \ge 0$.

results.title: Convergent numerators of the Hurwitz expansion
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $z$ be a complex number with Hurwitz partial quotients $a_0, a_1, a_2, \dots$. Its convergent numerators $P_n$, $n \ge 0$, are given by $P_{-1} = 1$, $P_0 = a_0$ and $P_{n+1} = a_{n+1} P_n + P_{n-1}$ for $n \ge 0$.

results.title: Convergent denominators of the Hurwitz expansion
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $z$ be a complex number with Hurwitz partial quotients $a_0, a_1, a_2, \dots$. Its convergent denominators $Q_n$, $n \ge 0$, are given by $Q_{-1} = 0$, $Q_0 = 1$ and $Q_{n+1} = a_{n+1} Q_n + Q_{n-1}$ for $n \ge 0$.

results.title: Legal indices of the Hurwitz expansion
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $z$ be a complex number with Hurwitz iterates $z_j$ and partial quotients $a_j$. A natural number $n$ is a legal index for $z$ when $z_j \ne a_j$ for every $j < n$, that is, when the Hurwitz expansion of $z$ has not terminated before step $n$.

results.title: Rounding error of the nearest Gaussian integer
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every complex number $z$, let $[z]$ be the Gaussian integer nearest to $z$, obtained by rounding the real and imaginary parts to the nearest integer with halves rounded up. Then $|\operatorname{Re}(z - [z])| \le 1/2$ and $|\operatorname{Im}(z - [z])| \le 1/2$.

results.title: The Fejér kernel
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $T > 0$ and, for $n \in \mathbb{Z}$, let $e_n(x) = e^{2\pi i n x / T}$ be the $n$-th Fourier character on the circle $\mathbb{R}/T\mathbb{Z}$. For a natural number $N$, the $N$-th Fejér kernel is the function $K_N : \mathbb{R}/T\mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{C}$ given by the Cesàro mean of the Dirichlet kernels, $K_N(x) = \frac{1}{N+1} \sum_{k=0}^{N} \sum_{n=-k}^{k} e_n(x)$.

results.title: Integrability of Fourier characters
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $T > 0$. For every integer $n$, the Fourier character $e_n(x) = e^{2\pi i n x / T}$ is integrable on the circle $\mathbb{R}/T\mathbb{Z}$ with respect to the normalized Haar measure, the Haar measure of total mass $1$.

results.title: Integral of a Fourier character
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $T > 0$ and, for $n \in \mathbb{Z}$, let $e_n(t) = e^{2\pi i n t / T}$ be the $n$-th Fourier character on the circle $\mathbb{R}/T\mathbb{Z}$. With respect to the Haar probability measure on the circle, $\int e_n = 1$ if $n = 0$ and $\int e_n = 0$ otherwise. This is the orthogonality of the Fourier basis.

results.title: The Dirichlet kernel has integral one
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $T > 0$, let $e_n(t) = e^{2\pi i n t / T}$ be the $n$-th Fourier character on the circle $\mathbb{R}/T\mathbb{Z}$, and for $k \in \mathbb{N}$ let $D_k = \sum_{n=-k}^{k} e_n$ be the $k$-th Dirichlet kernel. With respect to the Haar probability measure on the circle, $\int D_k = 1$; only the term $n = 0$ contributes, by orthogonality.

results.title: Symmetry of the Fejér kernel
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $T > 0$. For every natural number $N$ and every $x \in \mathbb{R}/T\mathbb{Z}$, the $N$-th Fejér kernel satisfies $K_N(-x) = K_N(x)$.

results.title: The Fejér kernel has integral one
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $T > 0$ and $N \in \mathbb{N}$. The $N$-th Fejér kernel $K_N$ on the circle $\mathbb{R}/T\mathbb{Z}$ satisfies $\int K_N = 1$ with respect to the Haar probability measure on the circle. This is one of the defining properties of an approximation to the identity.

results.title: Pointwise bound for the Fejér kernel
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $T > 0$ and $N \in \mathbb{N}$. For every point $x$ of the circle $\mathbb{R}/T\mathbb{Z}$, the $N$-th Fejér kernel satisfies $|K_N(x)| \le N + 1$.

results.title: Continuity of the Fejér kernel
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $T > 0$. For every natural number $N$, the $N$-th Fejér kernel $K_N$ is a continuous function from the circle $\mathbb{R}/T\mathbb{Z}$ to $\mathbb{C}$.

results.title: Integrability of the Fejér kernel

results.title: Products of Fourier characters
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $T$ be a real number and, for $n \in \mathbb{Z}$, let $e_n$ be the $n$-th Fourier character on $\mathbb{R}/T\mathbb{Z}$, given by $e_n(x) = e^{2\pi i n x / T}$ (the constant $1$ when $T = 0$). results.title: Reindexing a sum of Fourier characters, negative range
results.caption: Lemma
results.summary: Let $T > 0$, let $e_n(t) = e^{2\pi i n t / T}$ be the $n$-th Fourier character on the circle $\mathbb{R}/T\mathbb{Z}$, and let $N \in \mathbb{N}$. For every point $x$ of the circle, $\sum_{k=0}^{N} e_{k-(N+1)}(x) = \sum_{n=-(N+1)}^{-1} e_n(x)$.

results.title: Reindexing a sum of Fourier characters, positive range
results.caption: Lemma
results.summary: Let $T > 0$, let $e_n(t) = e^{2\pi i n t / T}$ be the $n$-th Fourier character on the circle $\mathbb{R}/T\mathbb{Z}$, and let $N \in \mathbb{N}$. For every point $x$ of the circle, $\sum_{k=0}^{N} e_{(N+1)-k}(x) = \sum_{n=1}^{N+1} e_n(x)$.

results.title: The sum of Dirichlet kernels is a squared modulus
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $T > 0$ and, for $n \in \mathbb{Z}$, let $e_n(x) = e^{2\pi i n x / T}$ be the $n$-th Fourier character on the circle $\mathbb{R}/T\mathbb{Z}$. For every natural number $N$ and every $x \in \mathbb{R}/T\mathbb{Z}$, put $G = \sum_{k=0}^{N} e_k(x)$. Then the iterated sum of Dirichlet kernels satisfies $\sum_{k=0}^{N} \sum_{n=-k}^{k} e_n(x) = G\,\overline{G} = |G|^2$.

results.title: Nonnegativity of the Fejér kernel
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $T > 0$. For every natural number $N$ and every $x \in \mathbb{R}/T\mathbb{Z}$, the real part of the $N$-th Fejér kernel at $x$ is nonnegative: $\operatorname{Re} K_N(x) \ge 0$.

results.title: The Fejér kernel as a squared modulus
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $T > 0$ and, for $k \in \mathbb{Z}$, let $e_k(x) = e^{2\pi i k x / T}$ be the $k$-th Fourier character on the circle $\mathbb{R}/T\mathbb{Z}$. results.summary: Let $T > 0$ and for $n \in \mathbb{Z}$ let $e_n(x) = e^{2\pi i n x / T}$ be the $n$-th Fourier character on $\mathbb{R}/T\mathbb{Z}$. Then for every $n \in \mathbb{Z}$ and all $x, t \in \mathbb{R}/T\mathbb{Z}$, $e_n(x - t) = e_{-n}(t)\, e_n(x)$.

results.title: Primitive word
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A nonempty finite word is primitive if it is not a proper power of another word.

results.title: Content of a word
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $r$ be a natural number. The content of a word $w$ over the alphabet $\{0, \dots, r-1\}$ is the function that assigns to each letter $i$ the number of occurrences of $i$ in $w$.

results.title: Lyndon word
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered alphabet, and order the words over $\alpha$ lexicographically. A word $w$ over $\alpha$ of length $n$ is a Lyndon word if it is nonempty and, for every $k$ with $0 < k < n$, $w$ is strictly smaller than its rotation by $k$, the word obtained by moving the first $k$ letters of $w$ to the end.

results.title: Content is additive under concatenation
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a natural number $r$, words $u$ and $v$ over the alphabet $\{0, \dots, r-1\}$, and every letter $i$, the number of occurrences of $i$ in the concatenation $uv$ is the number of occurrences of $i$ in $u$ plus the number of occurrences of $i$ in $v$.

results.title: Content of a one-letter word
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $r$ be a natural number. For every letter $i$ of the alphabet $\{0, \dots, r-1\}$, the content of the one-letter word $i$ takes the value $1$ at $i$ and the value $0$ at every other letter.

results.title: Content of a word after prepending a letter
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $r$ be a natural number, let $w$ be a word over the alphabet $\{0, \dots, r-1\}$, let $i$ be a letter, and write $c(u)$ for the content of a word $u$ (the number of occurrences of each letter in $u$). If $iw$ denotes $w$ with $i$ prepended, then $c(iw)(i) = c(w)(i) + 1$ and $c(iw)(j) = c(w)(j)$ for every letter $j \ne i$.

results.title: The content of a word sums to its length
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a natural number $r$ and a word $w$ over the alphabet $\{0, \dots, r-1\}$, summing over all letters $i$ the number of occurrences of $i$ in $w$ gives the length of $w$.

results.title: Words with prescribed content
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $r$ be a natural number. Given a function $d$ from the alphabet $\{0, \dots, r-1\}$ to the natural numbers, the words of content $d$ are the words $w$ over this alphabet whose content equals $d$, that is, in which each letter $i$ occurs exactly $d(i)$ times.

results.title: Lyndon words of given content
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a natural number $r$ and natural numbers $n_0, \dots, n_{r-1}$, the set of Lyndon words over the alphabet $\{0, \dots, r-1\}$, ordered as the natural numbers, in which each letter $i$ occurs exactly $n_i$ times.

results.title: Words of given content are counted by the multinomial coefficient
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $r$ be a natural number, let $n_0, \dots, n_{r-1}$ be natural numbers, and let $n = n_0 + \dots + n_{r-1}$. The number of words over the alphabet $\{0, \dots, r-1\}$ in which each letter $i$ occurs exactly $n_i$ times is the multinomial coefficient $\binom{n}{n_0, \ldots, n_{r-1}} = \frac{n!}{n_0! \cdots n_{r-1}!}$.

results.title: Primitivity via distinct rotations
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $w$ be a word of length $n$, and for $0 \le k < n$ let $w_k$ be the rotation of $w$ by $k$, obtained by moving the first $k$ letters of $w$ to the end. Then $w$ is primitive if and only if $w$ is nonempty and the $n$ words $w_0, w_1, \dots, w_{n-1}$ are pairwise distinct.

results.title: Nontrivial rotations move a primitive word
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If $w$ is a primitive word of length $n$ and $0 < k < n$, then the rotation of $w$ by $k$, obtained by moving the first $k$ letters of $w$ to the end, is different from $w$.

results.title: Primitive words of given content
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a natural number $r$ and natural numbers $n_0, \dots, n_{r-1}$, the set of primitive words over the alphabet $\{0, \dots, r-1\}$ in which each letter $i$ occurs exactly $n_i$ times.

results.title: Lyndon words are primitive
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Every Lyndon word over a linearly ordered alphabet is primitive.

results.title: Zero-based preferences of a word
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $w = w_1 \cdots w_{2n}$ be a word of natural numbers, read as the preferences of $2n$ cars for spots numbered $0, \dots, 2n - 1$. Car $i \in \{1, \dots, 2n\}$ prefers the spot $(w_i - 1) \bmod 2n$, where $w_i - 1$ is truncated at $0$. When every $w_i$ lies in $\{1, \dots, 2n\}$, for example when $w$ is a Stirling permutation of order $n$, this is the spot $w_i - 1$, which is spot $w_i$ in the one-based numbering.

results.title: Total displacement of a word
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $w = w_1 \cdots w_{2n}$ be a word of natural numbers, and for $i \in \{1, \dots, 2n\}$ let $d(i)$ be the displacement of car $i$ in $w$. The total displacement of $w$ is $d(w) = \sum_{i=1}^{2n} d(i)$.

results.title: Admissible lucky sets
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $n$ be a natural number. A finite set $S$ of natural numbers is an $n$-admissible lucky set if $S = \mathrm{Lucky}(w)$ for some Stirling permutation $w$ of order $n$, where $\mathrm{Lucky}(w)$ is the set of lucky cars of $w$.

results.title: Lucky sets of 1122 and 1221
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Read as parking functions of length $4$, the Stirling permutation $1122$ has car $1$ as its only lucky car, and $1221$ has exactly cars $1$ and $2$ lucky: $\mathrm{Lucky}(1122) = \{1\}$ and $\mathrm{Lucky}(1221) = \{1, 2\}$.

results.title: Displacement compositions of 1122 and 11244233
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The displacement composition of a word $w = w_1 \cdots w_{2n}$ is $\mathrm{dis}(w) = (d(1), \dots, d(2n))$, where $d(i)$ is the displacement of car $i$. For the Stirling permutations $1122$ of order $2$ and $11244233$ of order $4$, $\mathrm{dis}(1122) = (0, 1, 1, 2)$ and $\mathrm{dis}(11244233) = (0, 1, 1, 0, 1, 4, 4, 5)$ (the paper's Example 5.5).

results.title: Basic properties of lucky cars
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $n \ge 1$ and let $w$ be a Stirling permutation of order $n$, read as a parking function of length $2n$. Then (a) car $1$ is lucky; (b) the first car $i$ with $w_i = 1$ is lucky; (c) the number of lucky cars of $w$ is at least $1$ and at most $n$.

results.title: Characterization of extremely unlucky Stirling permutations
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $n \ge 1$ and let $w$ be a Stirling permutation of order $n$, read as a parking function of length $2n$. Then car $1$ is the only lucky car of $w$ if and only if for every $x \in \{2, \dots, n\}$ and every position $i \le x$, we have $w_i < x$.

results.title: Counting extremely unlucky Stirling permutations
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every integer $n \ge 1$, the number of Stirling permutations $w$ of order $n$ that are extremely unlucky, that is, whose only lucky car is car $1$ ($\mathrm{Lucky}(w) = \{1\}$), is $(n - 1)!$.

results.title: Characterization of extremely lucky Stirling permutations
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $w$ be a Stirling permutation of order $n$, read as a parking function of length $2n$. Then $w$ has exactly $n$ lucky cars if and only if the second occurrences of the letters of $w$ appear in decreasing order: for all positions $a < b$ such that $w_a$ also occurs before position $a$ and $w_b$ also occurs before position $b$, we have $w_b < w_a$.

results.title: Extremely lucky Stirling permutations and Dyck words
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every natural number $n$, there is a bijection between the Stirling permutations $w$ of order $n$ that are extremely lucky, that is, whose set $\mathrm{Lucky}(w)$ of lucky cars has exactly $n$ elements, and the Dyck words of semilength $n$ (valid parenthesizations of $n$ pairs of parentheses).

results.title: Extremely lucky Stirling permutations are counted by the Catalan numbers
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every positive integer $n$, the number of Stirling permutations $w$ of order $n$ that are extremely lucky, that is, whose set $\mathrm{Lucky}(w)$ of lucky cars has exactly $n$ elements, is the Catalan number $C_n$.

results.title: Extending admissible lucky sets
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $n \ge 1$. If $S$ is an $n$-admissible lucky set, then both $S$ and $S \cup \{2n + 1\}$ are $(n + 1)$-admissible lucky sets.

results.title: Necessary conditions for admissible lucky sets
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $n \ge 1$. If $S$ is an $n$-admissible lucky set, then $1 \in S$ and $2n \notin S$.

results.title: Parking before the second lucky car
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $w = w_1 \cdots w_{2n}$ be a Stirling permutation of order $n$, read as a parking function of length $2n$, and let $x$ be a lucky car of $w$ such that exactly one lucky car of $w$ is smaller than $x$, so that $x$ is the second-smallest element of the lucky set $\mathrm{Lucky}(w)$. Then every car $c$ with $2 \le c \le x - 1$ parks in spot $w_1 + c - 1$.

results.title: Left-to-right minima of a Stirling permutation sit at odd positions
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $w = w_1 \cdots w_{2n}$ be a Stirling permutation of order $n$ and let $j \in \{1, \dots, 2n\}$. If $w_j < w_i$ for every $i < j$, then $j$ is odd.

results.title: A second lucky car beyond $n$ is odd
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $w = w_1 \cdots w_{2n}$ be a Stirling permutation of order $n$, read as a parking function of length $2n$, and let $x$ be a lucky car of $w$ such that exactly one lucky car of $w$ is smaller than $x$, so that $x$ is the second-smallest element of the lucky set $\mathrm{Lucky}(w)$. If $x > n$, then $x$ is odd.

results.title: The first preference bounds the lucky cars
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $w$ be a Stirling permutation of order $n$, read as a parking function of length $2n$, with at least $3$ lucky cars, and let $x$ be the second-smallest lucky car of $w$. If $x \ge n$, then the number of lucky cars of $w$ is at most $w_1$, and every lucky car parks in one of the spots $1, \dots, w_1$.

results.title: When the penultimate car is lucky
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $n \ge 1$ and let $w = w_1 \cdots w_{2n}$ be a Stirling permutation of order $n$, read as a parking function of length $2n$. Then car $2n - 1$ is lucky, that is, belongs to the lucky set $\mathrm{Lucky}(w)$, if and only if $w_{2n-1} = 1$.

results.title: Admissible lucky sets with two elements
results.caption: Theorem

results.title: Counting admissible lucky sets with two elements
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every integer $n \ge 1$, the number of $n$-admissible lucky sets with exactly two elements is $n - 1 + \lceil (n - 1)/2 \rceil$.

results.title: Total displacement of a Stirling permutation is invariant under rearrangement
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $w = w_1 \cdots w_{2n}$ be a Stirling permutation of order $n$ and let $\sigma$ be a permutation of $\{1, \dots, 2n\}$. results.summary: For a probability distribution $\pi$ on $\alpha$ (the target) and a proposal $Q$ assigning to each $x \in \alpha$ a probability distribution $Q(x, \cdot)$ on $\alpha$, one Metropolis–Hastings step from $x$ is the distribution of the following move: draw $y$ from $Q(x, \cdot)$, then move to $y$ with the Metropolis–Hastings acceptance probability $a(x, y)$, and otherwise stay at $x$.

results.title: Detailed balance for Metropolis–Hastings
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\pi$ be a probability distribution on a type $\alpha$, $Q$ a proposal assigning to each $x \in \alpha$ a probability distribution $Q(x, \cdot)$ on $\alpha$, and $P(x, y)$ the probability that one Metropolis–Hastings step for target $\pi$ and proposal $Q$ moves from $x$ to $y$. Then $\pi(x) P(x, y) = \pi(y) P(y, x)$ for all $x, y \in \alpha$.

results.title: Normalizer of the conditional law
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $\pi$ be a probability distribution on the configurations $x : \iota \to S$, with $\iota$ and $S$ finite. For a coordinate $i \in \iota$ and a configuration $x$, the normalizer is $Z_i(x) = \sum_{s \in S} \pi(x[i \mapsto s]) \in [0, \infty]$, where $x[i \mapsto s]$ is $x$ with coordinate $i$ set to $s$. It normalizes the conditional law of coordinate $i$ given the other coordinates of $x$.

results.title: Gibbs update
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $\pi$ be a probability distribution on the configurations $x : \iota \to S$, with $\iota$ and $S$ finite, such that $\pi(x) \neq 0$ for every $x$. The Gibbs update of coordinate $i \in \iota$ from $x$ is the probability distribution of $x[i \mapsto s]$, the configuration $x$ with coordinate $i$ set to $s$, where $s$ is drawn from the conditional law of coordinate $i$ given the other coordinates of $x$.

results.title: Symmetry of differing in one coordinate
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For functions $x, y : \iota \to S$ and a coordinate $i \in \iota$, if setting coordinate $i$ of $x$ to $y(i)$ gives $y$, then setting coordinate $i$ of $y$ to $x(i)$ gives $x$.

results.title: Detailed balance for a Gibbs update
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\pi$ be a probability distribution on the configurations $x : \iota \to S$, with $\iota$ and $S$ finite, such that $\pi(x) \neq 0$ for every $x$, and for a coordinate $i$ let $P_i(x, y)$ be the probability that the Gibbs update of coordinate $i$ moves $x$ to $y$. Then $\pi(x) P_i(x, y) = \pi(y) P_i(y, x)$ for all configurations $x$ and $y$.

results.title: Gibbs updates are reversible
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\pi$ be a probability distribution on the configurations $x : \iota \to S$, with $\iota$ and $S$ finite, such that $\pi(x) \neq 0$ for every $x$. For every coordinate $i$, the Markov kernel $K$ of the Gibbs update of coordinate $i$ is reversible with respect to $\pi$: for all measurable sets $A$ and $B$ of configurations, $\int_A K(x, B) \, d\pi(x) = \int_B K(x, A) \, d\pi(x)$.

results.title: Systematic-scan Gibbs sampler
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $\pi$ be a probability distribution on the configurations $x : \iota \to S$, with $\iota$ and $S$ finite, such that $\pi(x) \neq 0$ for every $x$. For a list $l = (i_1, \dots, i_n)$ of coordinates, the systematic-scan Gibbs sampler is the Markov kernel on configurations that applies the Gibbs updates of the coordinates $i_1, i_2, \dots, i_n$ in this order; for the empty list it is the identity kernel.

results.title: A full Gibbs sweep leaves the target stationary
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\pi$ be a probability distribution on the configurations $x : \iota \to S$, with $\iota$ and $S$ finite, such that $\pi(x) \neq 0$ for every $x$. For every finite list $l$ of coordinates, in any order and possibly with repetitions, $\pi$ is an invariant measure of the systematic-scan Gibbs sampler that updates the coordinates in the order of $l$.

results.title: Probabilities of a finite law sum to one
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The probabilities of a law on a finite type, as reals, sum to `1`.

results.title: Metropolis–Hastings transition matrix
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The transition matrix `P(x, y) = mhStep π Q x y` of the Metropolis–Hastings chain, as a real matrix.

results.title: Metropolis–Hastings matrix is stochastic
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The Metropolis–Hastings matrix is stochastic.

results.title: Target is stationary for the Metropolis–Hastings matrix
results.caption: Theorem

results.title: Primitivity of the Metropolis–Hastings matrix
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a target with full support and a proposal with primitive transition matrix and symmetric support, the Metropolis–Hastings matrix is primitive.

results.title: The Metropolis–Hastings chain converges to its target
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Under the hypotheses of `isPrimitive_mhMatrix`, there are `C` and `0 ≤ ρ < 1` with `d_TV(Pⁿ(x, ·), π) ≤ C ρⁿ` for every start `x`.

results.title: Positivity of Gibbs sweep transition probabilities
results.caption: Theorem
